title: Erich Fromm: Humanistic psychoanalysis
overview: Syllabus Unit 2. Original concise theory notes, examples and a final six-criterion evaluation. The appraisals are study interpretations rather than numerical scores from a prescribed textbook.
objectives: Explain social character and the human dilemma

sections.heading: Social character and the human dilemma
sections.detailed: Fromm places personality within social and economic relationships. Social character links shared conditions of life with habitual ways of feeling and acting. His human dilemma concerns self-awareness, separateness and a search for connection. Unlike an account based only on instinct satisfaction, this approach asks how social arrangements shape what people want and value.

sections.heading: Existential needs and freedom
sections.detailed: Five needs organise the account: relatedness, transcendence, rootedness, identity and a frame of orientation. Freedom can bring isolation as well as opportunity. Authoritarianism, destructiveness and automatic conformity are escape routes; positive freedom preserves individuality while enabling connected, productive activity. These are theoretical explanations, not diagnoses of a person who values security.

sections.heading: Character orientations
sections.detailed: The nonproductive orientations are receptive, exploitative, hoarding and marketing. The productive orientation emphasises active, responsible engagement with life. Orientations describe patterns rather than fixed clinical categories. In an answer, distinguish receiving from others, taking from others, retaining possessions or feelings, and treating oneself as a marketable commodity.

sections.heading: Application and comparison
sections.detailed: Original illustration: a student chooses every activity solely to impress a group. Interpret this as possible conformity or a marketing orientation, then consider alternative explanations such as financial constraints or ordinary social learning. Compare Fromm with Freud on social versus instinctual emphasis, and with Horney on interpersonal and cultural conditions. An illustration demonstrates meaning; it does not verify the theory.

sections.heading: Evaluation using the six criteria
sections.detailed:
Generates research: Limited direct testing of the whole account; specific ideas about social character and consumer orientation can generate research questions.

Is falsifiable: Broad claims about human needs require precise measures and competing predictions before they can be disconfirmed.

Organizes data: Connects culture, individuality and social relationships, but its breadth can exceed the evidence available for particular mechanisms.

Guides action: Offers questions about conformity, autonomy and relationships; broad ideals alone do not specify a standard intervention.

Is internally consistent: Freedom, needs and character fit an overarching social account, although their definitions need careful separation.

Is parsimonious: A small set of needs is economical, but multiple orientations and historical assumptions increase complexity.

keyPoints: Assess specific claims, not whether a theorist was famous.

title: John Bowlby: Attachment theory
overview: Syllabus Unit 2. Original concise theory notes, examples and a final six-criterion evaluation. The appraisals are study interpretations rather than numerical scores from a prescribed textbook.
objectives: Explain attachment as a behavioural system
Explain bowlby and later attachment research
Evaluate the theory using all six criteria

sections.heading: Attachment as a behavioural system
sections.detailed: Bowlby explains attachment as a system supporting proximity to a protective caregiver, especially during threat. Attachment behaviour is not simply a side effect of feeding. A secure base supports exploration, while a safe haven provides comfort when distressed. Internal working models concern expectations about self and attachment figures; they guide behaviour but remain open to revision.

sections.heading: Development, separation and loss
sections.detailed: Early attachment develops through changing patterns of orientation, discrimination, proximity seeking and increasingly reciprocal partnership. Separation may activate protest and distress. The meaning and consequences depend on relationship history, duration, replacement care and the wider context. Avoid treating every separation as damaging or every early difficulty as an irreversible adult outcome.

sections.heading: Bowlby and later attachment research
sections.detailed: Bowlby’s theoretical contribution should be distinguished from Ainsworth’s observational methods and attachment classifications. The Strange Situation examines reunion and exploration under standardised conditions; it is not a universal personality label. Later classifications and adult measures are developments in the research tradition, not all inventions by Bowlby himself.

sections.detailed:
Generates research: Has generated extensive observational and longitudinal research; evidence about specific predictions should be distinguished from the entire tradition.

Is falsifiable: Caregiving, reunion behaviour and later outcomes can be operationalised, allowing predictions to be challenged.

Organizes data: Integrates protection, exploration and relationships across development, but does not explain every aspect of personality.

Guides action: Informs attention to continuity and sensitivity of care; intervention benefits require separate outcome evidence.

Is internally consistent: The behavioural-system and working-model ideas are connected; different attachment measures must not be treated as interchangeable.

Is parsimonious: A few organising ideas explain several behaviours, while developmental and contextual qualifications add necessary complexity.

title: Melanie Klein: Object relations theory
overview: Syllabus Unit 2. Original concise theory notes, examples and a final six-criterion evaluation. The appraisals are study interpretations rather than numerical scores from a prescribed textbook.
objectives: Explain internal objects and unconscious phantasy
Evaluate the theory using all six criteria

sections.heading: Internal objects and unconscious phantasy
sections.detailed: Klein emphasises early relationships as represented in the infant’s internal world. An object can mean a person or part of a person, rather than a physical possession. Unconscious phantasy concerns imagined relations, wishes and anxieties. Part-object and whole-object relations distinguish fragmented representations from recognising a person as containing both gratifying and frustrating qualities.

sections.heading: Paranoid-schizoid position
sections.detailed: Splitting keeps idealised and threatening aspects apart; projection and introjection help describe how experiences are attributed outside or taken inside. Persecutory anxiety concerns threat from bad objects. A position is an organisation of experience, not merely an age-bound stage. The term does not mean that every infant has a psychiatric disorder.

sections.heading: Depressive position and reparation
sections.detailed: Integration makes it possible to experience love and hostility toward the same whole person. Concern about harming or losing a loved object is connected with guilt and reparation. Movement between positions can recur under stress. The depressive position is a theoretical configuration, not synonymous with clinical depressive illness. Play analysis offers access to the child’s symbolic expression but interpretation needs caution.

sections.heading: Evaluation using the six criteria
sections.detailed:
Generates research: Influential in clinical thinking; claims about very early phantasy are harder to investigate directly than observable behaviour.

Is falsifiable: Flexible interpretations of symbolic play may accommodate contrary observations; independent predictions and coding improve testability.

Organizes data: Organises patterns of splitting, anxiety and reparation, but interpretive fit alone is not proof of explanatory accuracy.

Guides action: Offers a clinical language for relationships and defences, while interpretation and treatment outcomes need independent checks.

Is internally consistent: Concepts form a connected account; specialised meanings can be ambiguous without careful definition.

Is parsimonious: Part-objects, positions and several defence mechanisms provide detail at the cost of a more elaborate explanatory system.

flashcards.back: Klein emphasises early relationships as represented in the infant’s internal world. An object can mean a person or part of a person, rather than a physical possession. Unconscious phantasy concerns imagined relations, wishes and anxieties. Part-object and whole-object relations distinguish fragmented representations from recognising a person as containing both gratifying and frustrating qualities.

Splitting keeps idealised and threatening aspects apart; projection and introjection help describe how experiences are attributed outside or taken inside. Persecutory anxiety concerns threat from bad objects. A position is an organisation of experience, not merely an age-bound stage. The term does not mean that every infant has a psychiatric disorder.

Integration makes it possible to experience love and hostility toward the same whole person. Concern about harming or losing a loved object is connected with guilt and reparation. Movement between positions can recur under stress. The depressive position is a theoretical configuration, not synonymous with clinical depressive illness. Play analysis offers access to the child’s symbolic expression but interpretation needs caution.

title: David McClelland: Learned-needs theory
overview: Syllabus Unit 5. Original concise theory notes, examples and a final six-criterion evaluation. The appraisals are study interpretations rather than numerical scores from a prescribed textbook.

sections.heading: Achievement, affiliation and power
sections.detailed: McClelland studies differences in learned motivation, particularly achievement, affiliation and power. Achievement concerns meeting standards of excellence, affiliation concerns warm relationships, and power concerns influence or impact. The needs are dimensions that can coexist, not mutually exclusive personality diagnoses or a fixed sequence like a needs hierarchy.

sections.heading: Achievement motivation and incentives

title: Rollo May: Existential psychology
overview: Syllabus Unit 5. Original concise theory notes, examples and a final six-criterion evaluation. The appraisals are study interpretations rather than numerical scores from a prescribed textbook.
objectives: Explain love, will, care and intentionality
Evaluate the theory using all six criteria

sections.heading: Existence, freedom and responsibility
sections.detailed: May emphasises lived experience, choice, meaning and responsibility within real limits. Authenticity involves acknowledging one’s possibilities and limits rather than automatically surrendering decisions to expectations. Existential thought challenges explanations that reduce a person entirely to a mechanism; this philosophical emphasis must be distinguished from a directly testable scientific prediction.
sections.simple: May emphasises lived experience, choice, meaning and responsibility within real limits. Authenticity involves acknowledging one’s possibilities and limits rather than automatically surrendering decisions to expectations.

sections.heading: Anxiety, guilt and being-in-the-world
sections.detailed: Normal anxiety is proportionate to a threat and can be faced; neurotic anxiety is disproportionate and restricts action through defensive avoidance. Ontological guilt concerns neglected possibilities and relationships. Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt distinguish the surrounding world, interpersonal world and relation to oneself. These are conceptual perspectives, not clinical diagnoses or separate physical places.

sections.heading: Love, will, care and intentionality
sections.detailed: Care means that something or someone matters; will involves commitment to action. Love and will need integration rather than treating affection as passive and commitment as domination. May discusses sex, eros, philia and agape. Intentionality concerns the meaning-giving structure of experience, not merely having a conscious plan.

sections.heading: Evaluation using the six criteria
sections.detailed:
Generates research: Difficult to turn the entire account into precise hypotheses; related existential research is not automatically a direct test of May.

Is falsifiable: Broad meanings and personal experience make strong disconfirmation difficult unless a specific claim is operationalised.

Organizes data: Provides a broad framework for choice, meaning, anxiety and relationships, though interpretive coherence is not causal proof.

Guides action: Offers a therapeutic orientation toward responsibility and awareness, but less standardised procedural guidance than a manualised technique.

practice.q: Explain Rollo May’s existential psychology, illustrating the central concepts.
practice.answer:
Existence, freedom and responsibility: May emphasises lived experience, choice, meaning and responsibility within real limits. Authenticity involves acknowledging one’s possibilities and limits rather than automatically surrendering decisions to expectations. Existential thought challenges explanations that reduce a person entirely to a mechanism; this philosophical emphasis must be distinguished from a directly testable scientific prediction.

Anxiety, guilt and being-in-the-world: Normal anxiety is proportionate to a threat and can be faced; neurotic anxiety is disproportionate and restricts action through defensive avoidance. Ontological guilt concerns neglected possibilities and relationships. Umwelt, Mitwelt and Eigenwelt distinguish the surrounding world, interpersonal world and relation to oneself. These are conceptual perspectives, not clinical diagnoses or separate physical places.

Love, will, care and intentionality: Care means that something or someone matters; will involves commitment to action. Love and will need integration rather than treating affection as passive and commitment as domination. May discusses sex, eros, philia and agape. Intentionality concerns the meaning-giving structure of experience, not merely having a conscious plan.
